chunks: The Sheikh — may Allah the Exalted support him — informed me. He said: Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I heard Abu 'Abdillah (AS) saying:
When you enter the toilet, say: 'In the name of Allah, and by Allah. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the filthy corruptor, the impure filth, the accursed Satan.'
And when you exit, say: 'In the name of Allah. Praise be to Allah Who has granted me well-being from the filthy corruptor and removed the harm from me.'
And when you perform wudu, say: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. O Allah, make me among the oft-repentant and make me among those who purify themselves,'
'And praise be to Allah, Lord of all the worlds.' (Quran 1:2)
He then said: One must not face the qibla nor turn one's back to it; rather, one should sit facing east if one wishes, or west. And what indicates this is [as follows].

key_terms.التَّوَّابِينَ: the oft-repentant — those who constantly return to God in repentance (tawbah), echoing Quran 2:222
key_terms.الْخَبِيثِ الْمُخْبِثِ: the filthy corruptor — one who is intrinsically impure (khabith) and additionally spreads impurity to others (mukhbith); a compound epithet for Satan
key_terms.الْقِبْلَةَ: the qibla — the direction of the Ka'ba in Mecca, toward which Muslims face during salat
key_terms.الْمَخْرَجَ: the toilet, lit. 'the place of exit' — a euphemistic classical Arabic term for the lavatory

ai.seo_question: What supplications did Imam al-Sadiq (AS) prescribe for entering the toilet, exiting it, and completing wudu, and what is the ruling on facing the qibla during toilet use?
ai.summary: Transmitted through a complete chain from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) via Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, this hadith prescribes three liturgical supplications woven into acts of ritual purification: one upon entering the toilet, one upon exiting, and one upon completing wudu — each pairing the divine name (basmala) with specific petitions for refuge and purity. The hadith closes with a fiqh ruling that one must not face the qibla (the direction of Mecca) nor turn one's back to it while relieving oneself, directing the worshipper toward the east or west instead. Together these teachings embody the Shia principle that taharah is not merely a physical act but a state of constant spiritual awareness before God.
